articles.title: The Best 4K Gaming Monitors: OLED Leads, LCD Fights Back
articles.text:
The question is no longer whether a 4K gaming monitor can deliver sharp visuals and high refresh rates, but which display technology best suits your budget and how you use your PC. Unlike the GPU market, where hardware is now stubbornly expensive, 4K monitors have become far more accessible, with models now available across a much wider range of prices.
The market and our picks have been settled into four categories for choosing a new 4K gaming monitor: premium 32" OLEDs, more compact 27" OLEDs, mini-LED LCDs with genuine HDR performance, and affordable IPS displays built primarily for SDR gaming.
Every monitor listed here has been tested by us, and nearly all of them have full reviews either on TechSpot or over at Monitors Unboxed on YouTube. So our recommendations are based on hands-on testing, current pricing, and the trade-offs that matter in everyday use. Whether you want the best image quality available, high brightness without burn-in concerns, or simply a fast 4K monitor at a reasonable price, these are the models we would buy today.
Best 32-inch 4K Gaming Monitors
Asus ROG Strix OLED XG32UCWMG 32"
Right now, the best 4K gaming monitors on the market are 32-inch 4K OLEDs. Although 27-inch models are also available, I find the larger 32-inch panel size more immersive for 4K gaming, and prices are not much higher than those of the smaller models. These panels offer high resolutions, fast refresh rates, and excellent HDR performance for gaming. With two main panel types to choose from, QD-OLED and WOLED, there are plenty of great options, and it is rare to find one that is outright bad.
Unchanged from our previous buying guide, the Asus ROG Strix XG32UCWMG remains the best overall 32-inch 4K OLED. This is a 32-inch 4K WOLED with a 240Hz refresh rate, and we consider it the best option because of its excellent feature set. It uses a stunning glossy TrueBlack finish that is superior to glossy QD-OLED coatings and does a better job of preserving deep blacks across different viewing environments. QD-OLED has the persistent issue of blacks appearing gray in brighter rooms, which is a complete non-issue on the WOLED-based XG32UCWMG.
WOLED has two other advantages over QD-OLED. The first is better HDR performance, thanks to more consistent brightness output, no panel dimming in bright scenes, and peak brightness that still reaches 1,000 nits. A 4K 240Hz WOLED also supports dual-mode operation, allowing the monitor to run at 1080p and 480Hz. This mode offers excellent clarity for competitive gaming and adds versatility for those who play several types of games.
Asus also throws in several useful features, such as its Neo Proximity Sensor, OLED Anti-Flicker mode, ELMB, and unlocked color controls. QD-OLED does have some advantages, including wider color volume, higher color brightness, and better uniformity. However, we think the overall package offered by the latest glossy WOLED panels is the best on the market.
The XG32UCWMG is slightly cheaper in mid-2026 than it was last year, typically retailing for a little under $1,000. That is toward the higher end of 32-inch 4K pricing, but it is not outrageous compared with QD-OLED models that start at around $800. For those seeking a premium 4K model, spending around 25% more on this WOLED is reasonable, in our opinion.
More Bang for your Buck?
When it comes to value-focused QD-OLEDs, it is hard to go wrong because most offer excellent performance. In 2026, there are two main 32-inch 4K 240Hz panel variants: the original panel that launched in 2024 and an updated version introduced at the start of this year. The newer panel, which we tested in the Asus PG32UCDM Gen 3, has higher full-screen brightness at 300 nits versus 250 nits, slightly improved black levels in bright rooms, and 8% higher brightness in HDR content.
You can distinguish the new panel from the older version by its DisplayHDR True Black rating. The 500 tier indicates the 2026 panel, while the 400 tier indicates the 2024 panel.
Asus PG32UCDM Gen 3
The new panel is better, but not by much, so we do not think it is worth paying a significant premium. When a 2026 model is available for the same price as a 2024 model, by all means choose the newer version. However, monitors using the original panel are currently much cheaper. For example, the MSI 321UPX is available for just $800, while the new 322UR X24 is debuting at $1,100. In that situation, I would save the $300 and buy the older 321UPX.
MSI 321UPX
The 321UPX is the model we recommend in most situations because it routinely ranks as an excellent-value purchase based on our price tracking. There are, of course, several other models we have tested and liked, including the MSI 321URX, the curved Dell Alienware AW3225QF, and the Samsung G81SF for those who prefer a matte finish.
We suggest looking at the options available in your region and choosing the most affordable model with the features you need.
What's coming
When it comes to high-end 32-inch 4K OLEDs, the models we just discussed are available now and are products we would recommend buying today. However, you may also want to wait if you are interested in one of the WOLED options.
For example, our top pick, the Asus XG32UCWMG will soon be succeeded by a newer model, the ROG Strix XG32UQWMS. It has the same basic specs, including a glossy coating, a 4K 240Hz panel with a 1080p 480Hz dual mode, and the same RGWB subpixel layout. However, it is being upgraded to the latest Tandem WOLED technology, bringing higher brightness, DisplayHDR True Black 500 certification, and a rated peak brightness of 1,500 nits. It should become available at a similar price within the next few months.
There is also a new 32-inch RGB Stripe panel from LG that will soon debut in several monitors, including an Asus model called the PG32UCWM. We are not yet sure how that model will perform, but it is worth keeping an eye on because it is expected to launch in the near future.
Also coming as cheaper 165Hz models using both QD-OLED and WOLED panels. These displays do not offer motion clarity as strong as the 240Hz models. Outside of that difference, however, they provide performance that is largely identical to the full-fat 240Hz versions used in higher-end displays.
Normally, we do not think much of the 165Hz models because a $50 price difference compared with 240Hz alternatives is often insignificant. Recently, however, we have seen a model called the Asus ROG Strix XG32UCDS that offers a much more substantial discount. It costs just $600, which is $200 less than most 240Hz models. That is remarkably cheap for a 32-inch QD-OLED and makes it well worth considering when refresh rate is less important to you than OLED color performance.
Best 27-inch 4K Monitors with HDR
Dell Alienware AW2725Q 27"
For those who prefer a smaller 27-inch panel for HDR gaming, our recommendations are unchanged. The only available panel at this size uses QD-OLED technology and is essentially a smaller version of the first-gen 32-inch panels. That means you can expect similar performance to the larger models, but in a more compact format with higher pixel density.
The three standouts are the Dell Alienware AW2725Q, Gigabyte MO27U2, and MSI MAG 272UP X24. All three are typically available for between $650 and $700, use the same panel, and offer excellent value at those prices. It is difficult to recommend any of the more expensive alternatives unless you specifically need the additional features they provide.
The AW2725Q performs similarly to the other options. It is just as bright, looks excellent for HDR gaming, and uses a glossy panel that produces deep blacks. Its main downside is the lack of some features found on premium models, such as USB-C display input. It is usually my go-to choice in this category, especially when available for $700.
The MO27U2 is very similar to the AW2725Q in terms of overall performance and features. I was not as impressed with its highest-brightness HDR mode, which uses a boosted-brightness configuration rather than a more traditional Peak 1,000 mode. Outside of that, it performs similarly to other 27-inch QD-OLEDs. It also has an excellent design, USB-C connectivity, and a KVM switch, giving it a strong set of hardware features.
Gigabyte MO27U2
There is also the MSI MAG 272UP X24, a newer model that we have not tested, though we have confirmed that it uses the same OLED panel as the others. We have not seen any major feature differences compared with the Dell and Gigabyte models, and we expect it to perform similarly to the higher-end 272URX. However, it drops features such as DisplayPort 2.1, helping to keep the price down. With a typical price of $730 and recent sales reducing it to $700, it is definitely worth considering.
Several higher-end models are also worth considering for buyers seeking specific features, including the Asus ROG Swift PG27UCDM and ROG Strix XG27UCDMG. Some of these monitors include features that we do not think justify the higher price, such as DisplayPort 2.1, while others offer more useful additions, including the Neo Proximity Sensor found on both the ROG Swift and ROG Strix models.
Asus ROG Swift PG27UCDM
Finally, while 27-inch 4K QD-OLED displays offer excellent performance and remain easy to recommend, a competing 27-inch 4K WOLED panel is expected to enter the market shortly. We recently saw this panel at Computex and expect it to arrive soon. It uses Tandem WOLED technology, runs at 240Hz, and features an RGB stripe subpixel layout. It may be worth waiting to see how monitors using this panel perform before choosing a 27-inch 4K OLED for gaming.
Best 4K LCD Monitors with HDR
MSI, AOC, Koorui or KTC 27" Mini-LED
For those seeking a 4K HDR-capable LCD, our recommendations in this category remain unchanged as well from last year. We have not seen any new models arrive that would displace our previous picks, the current options still offer excellent value, and, as far as we are aware, all of them remain widely available.
There are three main reasons to choose a 4K HDR LCD gaming monitor. First, you may not want to deal with the potential burn-in concerns associated with OLEDs. For those who use their display for both gaming and productivity, LCDs are the safer choice and may offer better long-term durability.
Second, you may want a 4K HDR monitor without spending at least $700 on an OLED, as LCDs with mini-LED backlights are considerably cheaper. Third, you may simply prefer the extreme brightness that LCDs can provide, with current models pushing full-screen brightness beyond 1,000 nits.
MSI MPG 274URDFW E16M
The models we currently recommend are the MSI MPG 274URDFW E16M, AOC U27G4XM, Koorui S2741LM, and KTC M27P6, all of which appear to use the same panel. These are 27-inch 4K 160Hz IPS LCDs with 1,152-zone mini-LED backlights and support for a 1080p 320Hz dual-mode configuration. Unlike older models we have tested, this newer generation performs well and avoids the frustrating, deal-breaking flaws seen in some previous products.
With full-array local dimming, these 4K LCDs are genuinely capable of displaying HDR images properly, unlike fake HDR products that lack local dimming and are often marketed with misleading "HDR 400" specifications.
A 1,152-zone backlight allows for a substantial increase in contrast over SDR monitors, producing deeper blacks and reasonably precise control over bright and dark elements displayed at the same time. This creates the dazzling HDR effect you are paying for, rather than simply running the screen at a higher brightness level.
KTC M27P6
Speaking of brightness, these monitors are capable of extremely high output, particularly in brighter scenes. The KTC M27P6 reaches more than 1,700 nits in real-scene testing. Combined with good shadow detail and fast dimming response times, this produces strong HDR gaming performance that is a significant step up from cheaper SDR products. Under the right conditions, these LCDs can look remarkably similar to an OLED.
Motion performance is also quite good across these. They use typical fast IPS panels, with tuning that varies depending on the model. The KTC is well balanced across the middle of the refresh-rate range, while the AOC is better optimized toward 160Hz. The 1080p 320Hz dual mode improves clarity for competitive multiplayer gaming, making these versatile displays capable of HDR gaming in single-player titles, 320Hz gaming in multiplayer titles, and productivity work without burn-in concerns.
You can expect to pay between $400 and $500 for one of these monitors, representing roughly a 30% to 40% premium over basic 4K SDR models. As a mid-range 4K option positioned between SDR LCDs and OLEDs, that seems reasonable to us. We also do not have a strong preference among the four models at their current prices, largely because the differences are relatively small. They are typically priced within $50 of one another, with occasional discounts appearing from time to time.
AOC U27G4XM
The main deciding factor is whether you want the mini-LED backlight tuned more toward brightness or contrast. The KTC and Koorui models are the brightest and push peak brightness the hardest, occasionally at the expense of contrast.
The MSI and AOC models are still bright but favor stronger contrast and deeper black levels in HDR scenes. There is no right or wrong presentation, and we would recommend all four depending on pricing and availability in your region.
The other good news for buyers in this segment is that we are not expecting any major new releases throughout the rest of 2026. Based on what we have seen at trade shows and heard from monitor vendors, this generation of mini-LED technology is likely to remain the standard throughout the year.
Best Budget 4K Monitors without HDR
Gigabyte M27UP 27"
If what you want is a reasonably affordable 4K monitor for gaming, with perhaps some productivity work on the side, IPS LCDs offer excellent value. In the budget category, you will not find top-tier HDR hardware with advanced mini-LED backlights, but you will find excellent high-refresh-rate displays for SDR gaming.
The best option in this category is the Gigabyte M27UP, a 27-inch 4K 160Hz IPS LCD monitor. Although this display has an MSRP of $380, it is regularly available for around $330, at which point it becomes an excellent buy. Despite its low price, it delivers performance similar to other 4K IPS LCDs we have tested. It is reasonably fast, offers a well-tuned single overdrive mode, has good calibration, supports a wide color gamut, and delivers acceptable IPS-level contrast. The overall balance of performance makes the M27UP a great monitor for both gaming and productivity.
The other cool thing about this monitor is its 1080p 320Hz dual mode, which improves responsiveness and motion clarity for competitive gaming. Of course, you do not have to use dual mode. You could simply ignore the feature and enjoy the monitor's excellent value as a 4K display, but for those who play a wide variety of games, it is a worthwhile addition.
We do not recommend spending more than $330 on a standard 4K LCD, as the models we have tested generally offer a very similar level of performance in both motion handling and color quality. With the M27UP already well tuned for motion, well calibrated, and, in my opinion, well designed, there is little reason to spend more on something marketed as premium. You will probably just be wasting money, and once you move into higher price tiers, better options become available with more advanced display hardware.
Based on what we have seen over the past six months, the Gigabyte M27UP usually offers the best value in this category. However, there are a few alternatives worth watching, including the Asus ROG Strix XG27UCG, which is a very similar monitor. At the moment, the XG27UCG costs around $50 more than the M27UP, but if it goes on sale, we would simply buy whichever of the Asus or Gigabyte models is cheaper.
Asus ROG Strix XG27UCG
In previous versions of this buying guide, we also recommended several budget 32-inch 4K LCDs for SDR gaming. However, as of mid-2026, all of those monitors have been discontinued. The LG 32GR93U and Gigabyte M32UP are no longer widely available, apart from select retailers carrying old stock. We are also not particularly impressed with many of the remaining options, which for the most part are either underwhelming or too expensive.
With 32-inch OLEDs now falling toward the $600 range while offering 165Hz refresh rates, it becomes difficult to justify spending a similar amount on an LCD with the same refresh rate. Even for buyers who still prefer LCD, there are not many compelling options at that price. For now, unless the market changes later in the year, we cannot recommend a 32-inch 4K SDR LCD gaming monitor.

articles.title: Thinking outside the text box: Maple Scan founders launch Liquid Interactive with backing from AXL | BetaKit
articles.text:
The co-founders who encouraged shoppers to buy Canadian with grocery-scanning app Maple Scan have launched a new startup, focused on ushering in a new era of AI that’s more interactive than a standard chatbot conversation.
“The way we actually use [AI] has barely moved, and history says whoever closes that gap is who defines the era.”
Daniel Wigdor, AXL
Liquid Interactive, co-founded by Sasha Ivanov and Ben Pearman, came out of stealth on Tuesday morning with the launch of its Liquid Photos product and $700,000 CAD from Toronto-based venture studio AXL. The startup is developing patented technology to make photos, online demos, and visual assets more interactive. Its ultimate goal is to move beyond the way many people currently interact with AI: typing words into a text box and waiting for a long, verbose response.
“When we compare [text chatting] to other experiences online and in our lives, like video-based platforms on social media, it’s a lot less engaging and interesting,” Ivanov said in an interview with BetaKit. “There’s a lot we’re losing when we stick to text only.”
Liquid Interactive is launching with its first consumer app, Liquid Photos. The AI system pulls in photos you select from your camera roll and adds features to transform them into dynamic visual assets with generative AI. For example, a set of photos taken at the same place, around the same time, can appear connected in space and be rotated around in three dimensions despite the source photo being in two dimensions. Another feature can take an object and split it apart into its visual components so users can navigate its different parts. The company hopes to launch Liquid Photos on the App Store soon, but it’s currently available in beta to Apple and Android users.
For Ivanov, the current AI moment mirrors the advent of photography. “As people started to understand the medium and the new things they could do with it, it gave rise to things like film and cinematography,” he said.
Liquid Interactive is being incubated at AXL, a venture studio co-founded by University of Toronto professors that hopes to launch 50 AI startups in five years out of Canada.
Daniel Wigdor, AXL’s co-founder and CEO, wrote in an email to BetaKit that Liquid Interactive is an example of a startup using AI to “empower people to do what previously was impossible.”
“Today, AI can create bespoke experiences with deep understanding of the user, their understanding, their goals, their ways of seeing the world. And yet, the way we actually use it has barely moved, and history says whoever closes that gap is who defines the era,” he wrote.
Maple Scan, Ivanov and Pearman’s previous venture, notched more than 130,000 downloads amid the buy-Canadian frenzy that saw consumers shun American products amid an ongoing trade war. The app, which they created more as a consumer service than a for-profit business, is still operational, but they’re not focused on scaling it up.
Liquid Interactive’s launch comes as AI-generated visual content—from political ads to product photoshoots—has flooded the internet. The proliferation of these tools has raised concerns about impacts on workers: A 2026 report by the Future Skills Centre found that demand for entry-level and freelance creative labour may be reduced, as using AI to produce visual assets could create cost savings.
But Ivanov said Liquid Interactive isn’t trying to replicate and cut costs for what humans can already do. Instead, it wants to use AI to help make new ways to generate digital visuals, and “a creative team is an inherent part of that.”
“Our belief is that as content gets easier to generate, human judgement and direction become more valuable, not less, because someone still has to decide what is worth making and what is actually good,” he told BetaKit in an email. “We’re interested in putting power into the hands of the people doing those entry-level jobs to create art that would previously have been out of reach.”
He and Pearman hope to eventually sell their technology to operating system providers like Apple, and have their features incorporated into camera roll apps. They’re also demoing with brands that want their online stores and product rooms to be more interactive, for example, integrating product info and allowing users to navigate 3D video assets of products they are shopping for, with real-life product info involved.
Ivanov added that they work with a brand’s pre-existing assets, which were created by the company’s photography and graphic design team, then build on top of that.
“Our goal right now is to work with as many brands as possible to really test this out and get it into people’s hands,” Ivanov said.
Feature image courtesy Unsplash. Photo by David Veksler.

articles.title: Diagrid gives failed AI agents a way to resume
articles.text:
Diagrid gives failed AI agents a way to resume
AI agents can impress in a demo and still fumble in production. Diagrid’s Catalyst 2.0 aims to make them more resilient — and their actions tamper-evident — for high-stakes work.
With the launch of Catalyst 2.0, Diagrid on Tuesday has added a durable execution and attestation layer to agents built with LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, Google’s Agent Development Kit, OpenAI Agents SDK, and other popular frameworks.
The point here, the company notes, isn’t to get developers to adopt yet another agent framework. Instead, Catalyst runs underneath the existing frameworks and turns the agent’s model calls, tool calls, and handoffs into steps in a durable workflow. Diagrid says this allows an agent to resume from its last completed step when it’s interrupted, without having to repeat the entire run from step one.
“If the agent gets a prompt and it chooses to run 100 tools for the job and it fails at the 99th, it really needs to start back up from 99,” Diagrid co-founder and CTO Yaron Schneider tells The New Stack.
Picking back up at tool call 99
Catalyst is built on the open source Distributed Application Runtime (Dapr), which the Diagrid team helped build at Microsoft, and its built-in workflow engine. For each supported agent framework, Diagrid provides a runner that intercepts the framework’s execution loop and registers its operations as workflow activities.
“We hooked into their agent runner lifecycle, and we’re essentially able to take the agentic steps that are being executed in real time and register them as workflow steps for our workflow engine in Catalyst,” Schneider says.
In a LangGraph application, for example, a developer compiles the graph as usual and passes it to Diagrid’s DaprWorkflowGraphRunner. Catalyst records the inputs and outputs of the model and tool calls. Dapr’s workflow runtime can then replay the orchestration after a crash, while returning the stored results of completed activities instead of executing them again.
It’s worth noting that for LangGraph users, this isn’t the first form of durable execution. LangGraph’s own persistence layer saves state at superstep boundaries and supports resuming from the last successful step. Its Agent Server also provides a durable task queue and persistent checkpoints.
Diagrid’s argument is that Catalyst provides the same execution model across more than 10 frameworks and extends it to individual model and tool calls, without requiring developers to build separate recovery logic for each framework. Schneider says LangGraph is “without a doubt, hands down” the most common framework among Diagrid’s customers, with AWS Strands and Microsoft Agent Framework also showing up. All the other supported frameworks, he says, are in the long tail but easy enough to support that it makes sense for Diagrid.
A signed record of the run
There is a second part to Catalyst 2.0, though, which may be just as important for many enterprise users. With this update, the tool now brings the workflow-history signing features introduced in Dapr 1.18 to the supported agent frameworks.
“We keep like a ledger, like a diary,” Schneider says. “We log the input, we log the output, we log which systems we talk to.”
He describes the result as an immutable store but also notes that Catalyst doesn’t turn an arbitrary database into a blockchain. It creates a signed history that should reveal later modification.
Dapr computes a SHA-256 digest over batches of workflow-history events, links each digest to the previous signature, and signs the result with the Dapr sidecar’s Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone (SPIFFE) identity. It stores these signatures and certificates alongside the workflow history and verifies the chain whenever it loads the workflow state. If somebody were to modify, remove, or reorder a stored event, that verification chain breaks.
Schneider says Catalyst customers can use their own certificates and retain the encrypted history so it can be inspected even if they are no longer running Catalyst. The platform can use a customer-selected database, while the hash chain supplies the tamper evidence.
One part of the compliance problem
Diagrid is positioning that tamperproof record as useful for financial services, health care, and other regulated industries. CEO Mark Fussell says some of the financial executives the company has talked to see the lack of a verifiable record as a blocker for deploying agents in sensitive workflows.
The European Union’s AI Act is another reason Diagrid is making this argument now. Article 12 of the AI Act requires high-risk AI systems to support automatic event logging so operators can trace their behavior, identify risks, and monitor deployed systems, and a signed execution history could help with that requirement.
Fussell says Catalyst is meant to run alongside the agent services enterprises already use from the cloud providers. Teams can keep a provider’s identity, evaluation, and observability systems while using Catalyst for recovery and signed workflow history. Catalyst can run as a Diagrid-hosted service or in a customer’s environment, including air-gapped deployments.
Diagrid didn’t disclose pricing for the new release.

articles.title: Ninja Slushi Twist : la machine à granités ultime double la dose pour l'été
articles.text:
Ninja Slushi Twist : la machine à granités ultime double la dose pour l'été
Ninja élargit sa gamme de machines à granités avec la Slushi Twist. Doté de deux cuves indépendantes d'une capacité totale de 4,4 l, de la technologie de refroidissement automatisé Slush Assist et d'un système de distribution en tourbillon, ce nouveau modèle vise à faciliter la préparation simultanée de deux boissons glacées.
L’été bat son plein et, forcément, c’est le coup de feu pour les préparations glacées les plus gourmandes. Ninja arrive au cœur de la saison avec une proposition destinée aux grandes tablées et aux boissons instagrammables, puisque la marque décline sa Slushi en une mouture baptisée Twist qui promet de doubler la dose. Cette cousine de la Slushi Max, avec laquelle elle partage son bloc moteur de 440 W, embarque ainsi deux cuves.
La promesse est double : il est désormais possible de réaliser deux recettes différentes simultanément ou, lorsque les convives sont nombreux, de lancer deux fournées d’un même granité en parallèle. Pour ce faire, l’appareil inclut deux bacs de 2,2 l, soit un total de 4,4 l identique à la capacité maximale de la Slushi Max — pour une capacité utile de 2,8 l. La grande différence avec le modèle Max réside dans la flexibilité : la Twist accueille une ou deux recettes au choix (il est d’ailleurs possible de n’utiliser qu’une cuve pour une petite quantité), tout en automatisant la température de refroidissement.
Préparation automatisée et tourbillons glacés
Au lieu de laisser l’utilisateur choisir le mode adapté à sa recette, la machine se charge de détecter la rapidité de refroidissement et la texture des liquides qui lui sont proposés pour appliquer le réglage nécessaire. La technologie prend le nom de Slush Assist et ambitionne d’optimiser le temps de refroidissement pour des recettes prêtes encore plus rapidement. Comme avec les précédentes générations de Slushi, ce temps varie selon les ingrédients intégrés ; plus la boisson est sucrée, plus la cristallisation est rapide, tandis que la présence d’alcool ralentit le processus.
L’autre nouveauté de la Slushi Twist se cache dans son nom : elle permet de créer des tourbillons de boissons dans le verre. Pour ce faire, Ninja ajoute aux verseurs droits classiques deux becs incurvés vers le centre de l’appareil. Le verre est placé sur un plateau d’égouttage rotatif — l’opération n’est pas motorisée, puisqu’il faut adapter la vitesse de rotation à la texture des préparations.
Résultat, du moins pour les plus doués : des spirales de boissons glacées, qu’il vaut mieux réserver à des préparations aux couleurs contrastées. Ninja n’abandonne pas ses clients aux affres des granités ratés et leur suggère des associations gourmandes et photogéniques dans un livret fourni avec son appareil.

articles.title: Avec iOS 26.6, Apple corrige près de 90 failles de sécurité, mettez à jour votre iPhone !
articles.text:
Apple vient de lancer le déploiement de la mise à jour iOS 26.6 sur tous les iPhone et iPad compatibles. Cette nouvelle version du système d’exploitation comprend une poignée de nouveautés, dont la plupart préparent l’arrivée d’iOS 27 au mois de septembre 2026.
Une mise à jour lourde de correctifs
La mise à jour colmate surtout près de 90 vulnérabilités dans le code d’iOS. L’avis de sécurité publié par Apple recense 78 entrées de vulnérabilités distinctes, correspondant à 87 identifiants de failles de sécurité. Cet écart s’explique simplement par le fait que certains correctifs traitent plusieurs failles à la fois.
iOS 26.6 fait partie des mises à jour les plus chargées en correctifs de sécurité de ces dernières années. Historiquement, les mises à jour mineures d’iOS se limitent souvent à une quinzaine ou une vingtaine de correctifs. Comme prévu, Apple a décidé de déployer ses correctifs de plus en plus rapidement pour couper l’herbe sous le pied des hackers. Sur l’ensemble des systèmes Apple mis à jour, ce sont 194 failles de sécurité qui viennent d’être colmatées.
À lire aussi : Apple change de stratégie pour contrer les pirates et protéger votre iPhone
Des failles dans le cœur d’iOS
Quatorze failles concernent directement le noyau du système iOS. Parmi ces vulnérabilités, on trouve dix défaillances qui pourraient être exploitées pour faire planter un appareil. D’autres failles du noyau, à savoir le programme central qui fait le lien entre le matériel de l’appareil et tous les logiciels qui tournent sur l’iPhone, peuvent aboutir à un accès non autorisé à des données sensibles, voire à une modification de la mémoire du système.
On trouve aussi huit vulnérabilités dans WebKit, le moteur qui affiche les pages web sur les appareils Apple, et fait tourner Safari. Cible de choix pour les pirates, le moteur pouvait notamment être exploité pour espionner les contenus consultés par les internautes. Enfin, Apple a aussi comblé une faille dans Recopie de l’iPhone, la fonction permettant de contrôler son iPhone depuis un Mac. Un attaquant disposant d’un accès physique à l’appareil aurait pu s’en servir pour s’emparer de données personnelles. Citons aussi les trois correctifs intégrés à l’application Contacts. L’un des correctifs empêche qu’une fiche de contact piégée par un pirate ne vole des informations sensibles lorsqu’elle est ajoutée au carnet d’adresses. Un autre correctif bloque les applications qui tentaient d’ajouter des contacts sans demander l’accord de l’utilisateur.
À lire aussi : Apple muscle l’app Santé – iOS 27 traque désormais les signes de la ménopause
Bonne nouvelle, aucune des failles de sécurité corrigées par Apple n’a été exploitée par des cybercriminels. Le géant de Cupertino a pu agir en proposant des correctifs avant que les hackers ne découvrent les vulnérabilités. Néanmoins, on vous encourage à l’installer sur vos appareils sans tarder. La mise à jour peut être installée sur les iPhone 11 et les modèles plus récents, ainsi que sur de nombreux iPad compatibles. Pour en profiter, ouvrez Réglages, puis allez dans Général > Mise à jour logicielle, avant de toucher « Télécharger et installer ». Apple conseille, par précaution, de sauvegarder l’appareil, de le connecter au Wi-Fi et de vérifier que sa batterie atteint au moins 50% avant de démarrer l’installation.

articles.title: Over 24,000 exposed server BMCs leak password hash via decades-old flaw
articles.text:
More than 24,000 internet-exposed servers are leaking authentication password hashes due to a 20-year-old vulnerability in their Baseboard Management Controller (BMC) interface.
For at least a third of them, researchers were able to find the correct password using dictionaries and the patterns on factory stickers for default credentials.
The exposed servers are vulnerable to CVE-2013-4786, an IPMI 2.0 authentication weakness rooted in a protocol introduced in 2004.
The security issue allows attackers to request an authentication response that can be used to crack the password offline using dedicated GPU rigs or similar setups.
BMCs and server risks
BMCs are processors built into a server motherboard that allow administrators to remotely manage the system independent of the operating system. They support low-level actions such as powering servers on/off, updating firmware, or mounting virtual media.
Access to BMCs can give attackers control over physical servers, letting them change low-level configurations, apply malicious firmware updates, and compromise the system at a layer not monitored by security solutions.
Researchers at cybersecurity and infrastructure startup Lava say that in real-world settings, recovered credentials may work across multiple management interfaces within the same environment, and that a single compromised BMC could serve as a pivot point to the broader management plane.
In AI environments with poorly segmented infrastructure, attackers could affect multiple tenants simultaneously.
“A physical GPU server can support multiple tenants or workloads through virtualization, GPU partitioning, or other sharing mechanisms,” Lava researchers say.
“In those environments, compromise of one physical server could disrupt or expose several customer workloads.”
Massive exposure
Looking for publicly accessible IPMI services on UDP port 623, the researchers found 36,872 internet-exposed hosts. Of those, 24,650 exposed password-derived authentication material that could be used to perform offline password-cracking attacks.
According to researchers at Lava, 6,240 of the hosts accepted an empty username during authentication, and subsequent testing confirmed that they were also protected by weak passwords.
A number of 2,340 instances used weak administrator passwords that matched public dictionaries, making them very easy to breach.
On a live exposure map seen by BleepingComputer, the United States is at the top of the list with 39% of the vulnerable servers.
Lava researchers note that a large number of the BMCs it found exposed online are Supermicro systems protected by a 10-character uppercase password printed on the chassis label, with the username ‘ADMIN’ in all instances.
They argue that while this format theoretically provides ample headroom, its constrained structure still makes offline cracking practical.
For comparison, the researchers estimated that recovering an HPE factory password would take about 1 day per captured response (an authentication response obtained during the IPMI handshake) on an Apple M3 system.
Activity and response
Lava reports that during its research, it found an internet-exposed HPE iLO 4 login page displaying a ransom note demanding 0.3 BTC.
While this is not proof of widespread exploitation activity, or even successful attempts, it shows that at least some malicious activity is underway.
The researchers notified Supermicro in June, and while the company acknowledged the risk, it noted that official guidance for administrators recommends rotating default BMC passwords and isolating management networks.
The company, though, said it would review stronger default password policies for future hardware revisions.
Lava also notified HPE but received only a standard auto-response message and no follow-up from the vendor’s security team.
The researchers recommend keeping IPMI and Redfish off the public internet, rotating factory BMC passwords, restricting access to isolated management networks, and turning off legacy IPMI authentication.

articles.title: Logitech will pull a Nintendo — only European mice will come with replaceable batteries
articles.text:
In June, Nintendo announced a new version of the Switch 2 that should let you easily replace its battery pack — but only for Europe. Logitech will do much the same. User-replaceable batteries will be the law in Europe in February 2027, but instead of bringing them to the rest of the world, Logitech plans to ship one version of its wireless mice to Europe and a different version everywhere else.
Logitech will pull a Nintendo — only European mice will come with replaceable batteries
“Very few people will do this,” Logitech’s new gaming boss says.
“Very few people will do this,” Logitech’s new gaming boss says.
That’s the word from Logitech’s new gaming boss, Robin Piispanen. We talked about it over iced vanilla lattes at my local cafe, right after discussing how Logitech isn’t sure it wants to make another gaming handheld.
Why? Logitech believes that less-repairable peripherals might actually be superior, once you consider the tradeoffs.
“It’s not just the cost, you’re also adding weight,” Piispanen tells The Verge. He says that Logitech typically ships devices with a lightweight soft-sided lithium-based battery inside, with a very thin cable, because the company knows most people won’t take them apart. “But that is not safe for you to operate on, we can’t give that to you in good conscience and say, hey, go replace a soft-pack battery.”
Instead, Logitech’s wireless products in Europe will ship with a hard-pack battery, a more rigid design that’s harder to puncture accidentally. (Not to overstate the risk, but punctured lithium-based batteries can quickly start fires.) For extra safety, Piispanen says Logitech will offer certified replacement batteries in Europe, too.
But he says he won’t ship them to the United States, for example. He says Logitech ran the numbers, and its forecasts suggest few people will bother replacing those batteries.
“How many people are going to open up their own mouse, take out the battery, put in a new one because the battery ran old?” he asks. Piispanen says replaceable batteries make more sense for expensive products like laptops or phones, but that people tend to replace Logitech’s $50 to $100 wireless mice as they wear down.
While I agree that Logitech’s mice are currently disposable products, I strongly disagree that they should continue to be that way. Isn’t the right-to-repair movement about changing that outlook on the world? Would consumers change that behavior if the devices were easier to fix?
So I ask Piispanen, who says he believes in right-to-repair: Why doesn’t Logitech actually sell the wear-and-tear parts for its mice, despite claiming it does? Why doesn’t it sell the rubber grip pads on the side of my Logitech G502 Lightspeed, which I’ve now worn a hole through, or the mouse switch that’s beginning to double-click on the side of my mouse?
It sounds like the answer is: Logitech isn’t actually ready to trust consumers with repairs themselves.
“Mouse switches means you have to open up the whole mouse, and you’re most likely going to break something,” he says. Replacing the grips means cleaning up old adhesive and replacing it with new adhesive — “that’s a process for you to do it well.”
“I don’t want to like, sell you a part just for you to screw it up and then be sad about it,” Piispanen says later.
That said, he says he sees the passion in the community, how some people are willing to void their warranty to modify their Logitech gear, and he seems to take my point that Logitech isn’t fulfilling its “wear and tear” right-to-repair promise yet.
He says that “the bigger question” is how Logitech can design new products that don’t wear out as quickly. “The mouse you’re talking about, that was seven years old, and I salute you for really wanting to keep on using it,” he says.
But he also tells me he’ll take a look at those mouse grips: “I want to see what spare parts we’re lacking that is wear and tear, because if we’re talking about things that we actually could do, I want to look into that.”

articles.title: ¿Adiós a las operaciones de vista? Estas gafas inteligentes restauran la visión borrosa en pocos días
articles.text:
Europa acaba de aprobar el uso de unas nuevas gafas inteligentes que poco tienen que ver con las Ray-Ban Meta o las próximas de Apple Glasses. Estas no graban tu POV ni se pueden utilizar para conversar con la IA o escuchar música: su objetivo es restaurar los problemas de visión. Y no las dioptrías clásicas o el astigmatismo: prometen solventar la degeneración macular asociada a la edad (DMAE), una afección que las gafas o lentillas no pueden solucionar.
La idea es bastante sorprendente, la tecnología que hay detrás es sumamente avanzada y, aunque todavía está en fase experimental, ya ha sido aprobada para su comercialización gracias al éxito de las pruebas iniciales. Por el momento no hay precio ni fechas, pero ya sabemos cómo funciona y el porcentaje de mejora.
El sistema consta de dos partes: unas gafas inteligentes con un módulo de cámara que apunta a la retina del ojo afectado y un segundo componente en forma de chip que debe implantarse mediante cirugía en la zona ocular. Un conjunto algo engorroso y con mucho margen de mejora en el diseño, pero que soluciona un problema de visión irreversible y sin cura.
Así son las gafas inteligentes que curan la DMAE
El DMAE es una afección degenerativa totalmente relacionada con la edad. Según avanza, hace que el centro de la visión se emborrone y, cuando es severa, puede llegar a mostrar un punto negro completamente irreversible.
La idea de PRIMA es la siguiente: que las gafas inteligentes sean capaces de captar la imagen y enviar una serie de impulsos eléctricos al implante para que el cerebro los transforme en una imagen mucho más clara de lo habitual en pacientes que sufren DMAE. El proceso es continuo y automático, por lo que no es necesario hacer nada especial más allá de ponerse las gafas.
Por supuesto, el sistema requiere de una pequeña intervención quirúrgica para colocar el implante de 2x2 mm en su posición, además de una pequeña rehabilitación y una curva de aprendizaje y adaptación a las gafas inteligentes.
La buena noticia es que los resultados son impresionantes. El 81% de los pacientes intervenidos han experimentado una mejora significativa en la visión, pudiendo leer palabras que antes eran invisibles o muy borrosas.
La compañía está fundada por varios ex-Neuralink, la empresa de Elon Musk que ha conseguido avances significativos en la implantación de chips cerebrales para revertir ciertas enfermedades.

articles.title: OT Security Startup Frenos Raises $1.52 Million
articles.text:
AI-native OT security startup Frenos today announced raising $1.52 million in a seed funding round extension that brings the total raised by the company to $6.4 million.
The new investment round was led by Momenta and Exposition Ventures, with additional support from Riptide Ventures.
Frenos will use the new funding to expand its customer success team and to grow its AI R&D.
In addition to the fresh funding, the startup launched SAIRA Co-Work, an AI reasoning agent designed to provide evidence-based insights during complex investigations.
Founded in 2023, US-based Frenos has built an autonomous operational technology (OT) security assessment platform that continuously validates the security posture of OT systems.
The platform uses a digital twin of the customer’s network and SAIRA to run fully simulated penetration tests, validating attack paths, chaining exploits, and prioritizing risks.
According to Frenos, its approach reduces assessment time to minutes, has no downtime impact, requires no additional hardware or scanning, and is risk-free.
“Most OT security testing today tells you what’s vulnerable, not what’s defensible. The question that matters is what path takes an attacker from an exposed HMI to a process they can actually disrupt, and almost nobody is testing for that,” said Dragos co-founder and CEO and Frenos advisory board member Robert M. Lee.
“Frenos is one of the only teams I’ve seen build a platform that thinks in those terms without putting production at risk to do it. That’s a rare combination, and it’s why I joined the advisory board,” Lee continued.

articles.title: ASML se hunde en bolsa: el precio de que China empiece a fabricar su propia litografía
articles.text:
ASML ha encajado un golpe duro. Apenas unas horas después de que The Information revelara que una empresa china respaldada por el Estado había comenzado a fabricar en serie sus propias máquinas de litografía de ultravioleta profundo (UVP) de inmersión, las acciones de ASML se desplomaron. Cayeron hasta un 6,5% en Ámsterdam, su nivel más bajo desde principios de junio, mientras que en Wall Street llegaron a caer un 6,3%.
No obstante, cuando ASML estornuda otras compañías se resfrían. Y es que Applied Materials, Lam Research y KLA Corp, los otros grandes proveedores occidentales de equipos para fabricar circuitos integrados, se dejaron entre un 4% y un 7% en la misma sesión bursátil arrastrados por el mismo temor de fondo: que China, después de años intentándolo, empiece por fin a resolver el eslabón de la cadena de los semiconductores que más se le resistía.
Los medios internacionales todavía no han confirmado cuál es el nombre de esta empresa, aunque varios de ellos aseguran que reside en Shanghái (China), por lo que probablemente se trata de Shanghai Yuliangsheng Technology, una empresa emergente vinculada a Huawei y SiCarrier. Esto significa, sencillamente, que el ecosistema de proveedores que China ha ido tejiendo alrededor de Huawei durante los últimos años empieza a dar frutos también en fotolitografía. Sea como sea, el mercado ya ha decidido que la amenaza, aunque incipiente, es real.
El negocio en China de ASML se resiente
Este batacazo en las bolsas llega en un mal momento para el negocio de ASML en China. Sus ventas en este país asiático representaron el 19% de sus ingresos durante el primer trimestre de este año, y cayeron al 14% en el segundo. Aun así, esta compañía neerlandesa presentó unos resultados trimestrales sólidos: unas ventas netas de 9.326 millones de euros en el segundo trimestre, un 21% más que hace un año, y un beneficio neto de 2.918 millones, un 27% más con un margen bruto del 54%, ligeramente por encima del 53,7% del año anterior.
ASML todavía prevé entregar unos 130 sistemas de inmersión en todo el mundo durante 2026
Su director general, Christophe Fouquet, incluso elevó a mediados de julio su previsión de ingresos netos para 2026 hasta un rango de entre 43.000 y 45.000 millones de euros apoyándose en una demanda de chips de inteligencia artificial (IA) que sigue disparada. Esto significa, sencillamente, que ASML llega a este contratiempo con el viento a favor en su negocio principal, la litografía UVE, un segmento en el que China ni fabrica ni puede comprar sus máquinas más avanzadas. La UVP de inmersión, en cambio, sí puede fabricarla, lo que ha provocado precisamente el susto de este lunes.
Por otro lado, no debemos pasar por alto que ASML todavía prevé entregar unos 130 sistemas de inmersión en todo el mundo durante 2026, un volumen que la compañía china ni de lejos puede igualar con sus cinco unidades previstas para este año. Aun así, la simple posibilidad de que China deje de necesitar a ASML para producir los chips menos avanzados, los que necesitan los coches, los electrodomésticos y buena parte de la industria mundial, basta para que el mercado empiece a prever la llegada de un futuro distinto.

articles.title: Elon Musk's X Money app is rolling out in the US | TechCrunch
articles.text:
X is launching its X Money app for paid X subscribers in the United States.
Users get an X Visa debit card, which they can immediately add to Apple Pay and use to make instant peer-to-peer transfers within the app without fees or limits. They will also receive a physical X Visa debit card that, according to X Money, has no foreign transaction fees and offers free cash withdrawals at worldwide ATMs.
X Premium+ users (who pay $40 per month or $395 per year) are eligible for 6% APY, while Premium users (who pay $8 per month or $84 per year) can access the 6% rate if they link a direct deposit to their X Money account. X Money also says that users can get up to 3% cash back on certain purchases, and if they link a direct deposit, they can access that money a few days early.
The release of X Money reflects a decades-long dream for Elon Musk. In 1999, he founded X.com as a financial services startup, which later merged into PayPal. When he acquired Twitter in 2022, Musk changed the name of the platform to X and repurchased the X.com domain name.
Since the Twitter acquisition, Musk has repeatedly stated that he wants to turn the social platform into an “everything app,” and the rollout of X Money is part of that ambition.

articles.title: DITTO raises €5.2 million to tackle menstrual health gaps with research and targeted supplements | EU-Startups
articles.text:
DITTO, the scientist-founded menstrual health company, today announced a €5.2 million ($6 million) Seed round to accelerate its research projects, expand its science-led supplement range and increase its reach.
The round was led by FoodLabs, with support from returning investor EKA Ventures and a group of angel investors.
Alice van der Schoot, co-founder and Chief Scientist of DITTO, said, “Too many women are told their concerns are normal, or that they’re being dramatic, and sent away without answers. Until DITTO, there was nowhere for women to find research about what they were going through, or science-led solutions built for the reality of what they were living.
“We do the research ourselves, decode the studies explaining what women are dismissed for, and combine neuroscience and nutrition to build products grounded in evidence. That’s why our community has grown the way it has – women finally feel heard, are equipped with information to advocate for themselves, and they’ve found something that works.”
Founded in 2024 by neuroscientist and nutrition scientist Alice van der Schoot and ex- Brand Director at L’Oréal Adam Kugler, DITTO claims to be building an evidence-based menstrual health brand at the intersection of research, community and targeted solutions. The company states that its supplement combines clinical trials with advanced nutrient delivery biotechnology. It also translates emerging research for a community of over 300k.
According to the company, menstrual cycle and hormone-related symptoms have long been under-researched and under-discussed. Too many women are met with vague guidance, little reliable information, and walk away after their symptoms aren’t taken seriously.
“The challenges women face around their menstrual cycle arise from pathways that involve both the body and brain. PMS, premenstrual syndrome, is the mix of physical and emotional symptoms many women experience in the days before their period, from cramps and bloating to fatigue and low mood. PMDD, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, is far more severe and less recognised, where mood symptoms become intense enough to significantly disrupt daily life,” the company explains.
DITTO’s first product, Premenstrual Daily, is a supplement for women living with menstrual cycle-related challenges. The company states that it’s designed to work proactively, helping the body and brain build up resilience to the impact of hormone shifts before symptoms can take hold, rather than only addressing them once they arrive.
It further notes that the ingredients are selected for the strength of evidence behind them, then encapsulated using innovative nutrient delivery technology for maximum absorption.
DITTO reports that it has completed clinical trials on the finished formulation, in which 88% of women had significantly reduced symptoms.
The company has completed an initial clinical trial and is beginning to share results from it. A larger trial and a real-world evidence study are now in process. DITTO’s research extends beyond its supplement too, addressing historically overlooked areas that affect its community, including a systematic review into the links between PMDD and ADHD.
Flo Breiner, Operating Partner at FoodLabs, said, “DITTO is a research platform that develops and sells products. In the market of menstrual health, clinical evidence is becoming the price of entry, and the first company to set that standard is the one everyone else gets measured against. With proprietary delivery technology, a community of 300,000 women and a loyal customer base with strong retention, DITTO is that company.”

articles.title: Revolut macht Private Equity massentauglich: Doch die Anlageklasse hat ihre Tücken
articles.text:
Revolut macht Private Equity massentauglich: Doch die Anlageklasse hat ihre Tücken
Die britische Neobank Revolut bietet deutschen Kund:innen jetzt auch Zugang zu sogenannten Private Markets. Das sind Finanzprodukte, die nicht in börsennotierte Unternehmen, sondern in Private Equity, Infrastruktur und private Kredite investieren.
Zum Start öffnet Revolut direkt in der App den Zugang für Fonds der Vermögensverwalter Apollo, Hamilton Lane und Partners Group, die zusammen mehr als 2,2 Billionen Dollar verwalten. Die Fonds sind als ELTIFs (European Long-Term Investment Fund) strukturiert.
Was sind ELTIFs?
Fonds wie die von Apollo, Hamilton Lane und Partners Group waren lange institutionellen Anleger:innen vorbehalten. Privatanleger:innen konnten hier nur unter strengen Auflagen investieren. So mussten sie eine Mindesteinlage von 10.000 Euro aufbringen und das investierte Kapital durfte nicht mehr als zehn Prozent ihres Gesamtvermögens ausmachen.
Mit der ELTIF-2.0-Verordnung hat sich das aber schon im Jahr 2024 geändert. Die EU lockerte damals die Regeln für die Fonds, die in Infrastrukturprojekte, Private Equity und Kreditfonds (Private Debt) investieren.
Für Anleger:innen kann das spannend sein, weil Investitionen in solche Projekte und Unternehmen eine hohe Rendite versprechen. Allerdings bergen die Produkte auch Risiken.
Denn das Geld ist hier grundsätzlich langfristig gebunden, meist für sieben bis zwölf Jahre. Wer vor der Ablaufzeit darauf zugreifen will, muss Aufschläge zahlen, außerdem können die Fonds die Rückgabe jederzeit einschränken. Außerdem ist die Wertentwicklung des Fonds weniger transparent als etwa bei einem börsennotierten Fonds (ETF) und die Kosten sind meist deutlich höher.
So sieht das Private-Markets-Angebot von Revolut aus
Revolut betont, dass ein eigens dafür aufgebautes Team an Fondsspezialisten die Fonds kontrollieren wird. Dabei bewertet die Neobank unter anderem die jeweilige Anlagestrategie, den bisherigen Track Record, die operative Robustheit des Fondsmanagements und ob die Strategien sich in unterschiedlichen Marktphasen bewähren.
Außerdem soll es, anders als bei klassischen Privatmarktfonds, vierteljährliche Rückgabefenster geben. Anleger:innen können bereits ab einem Betrag von nur einem Euro investieren und ohne Ausgabeaufschlag investieren. Die Managementgebühr beträgt zwischen 1,65 und 2,35 Prozent pro Jahr, zudem ist eine erfolgsabhängige Vergütung des Fonds von zehn bis 15 Prozent, wenn bestimmte Renditeziele erreicht werden.
Revolut weist allerdings selbst darauf hin, dass die Fonds illiquide bleiben. Rücknahmen sind nicht garantiert und können je nach Marktlage oder Fondsbedingungen ausgesetzt werden. Daher richten sich die Fonds ausdrücklich an erfahrene Anleger:innen, die langfristig investieren wollen.
Mit dem Angebot setzt Revolut auf einen Markttrend, den auch Konkurrenten wie Trade Republic oder Scalable Capital bereits abbilden. Beide ermöglichen Zugang zu Private Markets. Trade Republic etwa bietet Fonds von Apollo und EQT an, Scalable kooperiert mit BlackRock.
Für die Fonds selbst ist der Zugang zu Privatanleger:innen spannend, zumal sie gerade unter Druck stehen. Ihr Kernklientel, also vermögende Privatkund:innen, hat zuletzt vermehrt Rücknahmeanträge gestellt, wie die Nachrichtenagentur Bloomberg berichtet. Apollo und Ares gehören demnach zu den Investmentgesellschaften, die Rücknahmen zuletzt eingeschränkt haben. Auch Partners Group beschloss im vergangenen Monat, die Auszahlungen aus einem großen Fonds zu begrenzen.

articles.title: Uber’s Zero Growth Stack: Scaling Services, While Optimising Infrastructure and AI Cost
articles.text:
Uber's "Zero Growth Stack" offers a scalable infrastructure solution that decouples capacity growth from business demand, allowing the company to reduce its physical hardware footprint while maintaining service scaling significantly. By prioritising automated runtime optimisation and rigorous AI lifecycle management, this strategic shift mitigates the overhead of traditional resource scaling. Central to this approach is a systematic transition toward dynamic system control, ensuring that infrastructure performance remains efficient even as internal software complexity increases.
A central pillar of this initiative is the systematic optimisation of Go runtime performance. Recognising that static garbage collection (GC) tuning often failed to address services with highly varied memory footprints—ranging from 100MB to 1GB—Uber engineered a dynamic solution: GOGCTunner. This library automates the adjustment of the GOGC value, which dictates the frequency of GC cycles relative to heap growth. By integrating directly with cgroup memory limits and monitoring live object utilisation, the tool enables dynamic runtime adjustments. While this automation successfully reclaimed 70,000 CPU cores across 30 mission-critical services, it replaces static settings with a control loop that must balance heap size (maintained at 1.25x live objects) against strict 70% memory utilisation thresholds to avoid OOM events.
Beyond infrastructure, Uber has integrated generative AI into its software development lifecycle to accelerate developer velocity. The architecture layers include a Platform Layer (utilising Michelangelo AI as a model gateway), a Context Layer (employing an MCP Gateway to inject internal source code), a Specialised Layer (deploying background agents like Minion and Shepherd), and a Review Layer (using tools like uReview and Code Inbox). While 92% of engineers utilise these agents monthly—with 31% of new code being AI-authored and Autocover generating over 5,000 unit tests per month—the rapid adoption introduced significant economic friction. AI-related costs increased sixfold since 2024, as token-based billing models led to budget exhaustion and individual developer costs reached $2,000 monthly by early 2026.
To address these challenges, Uber transitioned from unconstrained adoption to strict cost governance, implementing usage caps limited to $1,500 per developer. The company is now auditing the efficacy of AI-generated code, seeking to quantify the direct impact of automated throughput versus infrastructure overhead. To evolve these metrics, teams are shifting from aggregate cost tracking to granular indicators. Rather than relying solely on revenue per unit of labour and AI compute spend, the company suggests evaluating the "net code quality ratio", comparing the frequency of post-release hotfixes in AI-authored versus human-authored code. Establishing a "compute efficiency per feature" metric allows engineering leads to determine whether the overhead of AI-generated code—particularly when factoring in redundant tests generated by tools like Autocover—aligns with long-term infrastructure sustainability goals, ensuring that infrastructure optimisation remains synchronised with actual feature delivery.

articles.title: Ramp fully launches in Canada alongside new Toronto office | BetaKit
articles.text:
New York City-based FinTech giant Ramp has opened its corporate expense management platform to Canadian businesses as it plans to add a new Toronto office.
The news: After only serving a small number of businesses operating in Canada for the past couple of years, Ramp announced its expanded entry into the Canadian market on Tuesday. Its finance platform is now available broadly to Canadian-headquartered businesses outside of Saskatchewan and Québec.
Ramp bills itself as an all-in-one finance platform that uses AI automation to help companies with corporate cards in multiple currencies, expense management, reimbursements, bill pay, accounting sync, and more.
From the source: “Over the past year we’ve been hard at work at building Ramp for Canada,” Ramp VP of international expansion Jacob Wallenberg said in a LinkedIn post. ”We’ve customized the product to extract the local tax fields, and built financial products that help businesses who operate both in CAD and USD.”
Ramp’s new downtown Toronto office is also set to open in the first week of August. In an email to BetaKit, a Ramp spokesperson said that the company is initially hiring around a dozen employees for the Toronto office, with plans to double that figure over the next six months. They added that Ramp already has roughly 100 employees in Canada.
Following the thread: Ramp’s entrance was foreshadowed earlier this year when it began posting Canadian job listings on LinkedIn.
As it fully enters Canada, Ramp becomes one of the largest FinTech companies operating in the country, with over 70,000 customers, including Visa, Uber, and Shopify. The company’s annualized revenue reportedly exceeds $1 billion and, just last month, it raised a $750 million USD ($1.1-billion CAD) round at a $44 billion valuation.
Final thought: Until now, the Canadian corporate expense management market has been held by domestic players like Float and Venn, who also position themselves as built for the unique needs of Canadian businesses. Float recently eclipsed 7,500 Canadian business customers, and Venn says it supports more than 15,000, all of which Ramp will now be competing for.
UPDATE (07/28/2026): This story has been updated with details about Ramps’s Toronto office and Canadian hiring plans.

articles.title: Un fournisseur réclame 250 000 $ par semaine à Tesla pour débloquer la production du Cybertruck
articles.text:
Le Cybertruck continue d’accumuler les péripéties. Après la démonstration chaotique de 2019, les retards d’industrialisation, les rappels successifs et les ventes qui ne décollent pas, on pensait que Tesla avait déjà essuyé tous les plâtres. C’était sans compter sur une relation tendue avec un fournisseur qui tourne à la prise d’otage de pièces et de machines, bloquant la production du véhicule dans la Gigafactory texane.
Le 23 juillet 2026, Tesla a été contrainte d’attaquer en référé d’urgence l’entreprise Angstrom Automotive Group devant le tribunal. Le sous-traitant, au bord de la faillite, a décidé de bloquer les machines fabriquant des pièces du Cybertruck, selon le site spécialisé Teslarati. Et la situation s’envenime.
Les raisons du bras de fer entre Angstrom et Tesla
L’affaire commence le 13 juillet 2026 lorsque Angstrom Automotive prévient Tesla qu’elle s’apprête à fermer définitivement l’usine de Troy, au Texas, où sont fabriquées des pièces du Cybertruck. Sauf qu’au moment de discuter des modalités de restitution des équipements, tout ne s’est pas passé comme prévu.
Les machines logées dans l’usine (outils de fonderie sous pression, matrices d’ébavurage, dispositifs de fixation, outils de coupe, jauges et l’équipement de contrôle à rayons X) appartiennent pourtant juridiquement à Tesla. Le constructeur les avait mises à disposition du fournisseur qui, à l’époque, n’appartenait pas encore à l’entreprise Angstrom. Ce fournisseur a été racheté il y a un peu plus d’un an par Angstrom.
Selon les documents judiciaires, en plus des machines, Angstrom n’aurait pas livré 700 pièces finies qui auraient dû quitter l’entrepôt le 17 juillet pour alimenter les chaînes de production de Tesla.
Le 21 juillet, Tesla dépêche une équipe sur place, flanquée d’agents du shérif local pour récupérer son matériel. Le fournisseur leur refuse simplement l’accès. Selon la plainte déposée par le constructeur, le sous-traitant aurait alors exigé 250 000 dollars par semaine pour maintenir le site ouvert ou libérer les machines. Une demande qualifiée d’extorsion commerciale par les avocats de Tesla.
Ne voyant aucune autre issue, Tesla a opté pour la voie judiciaire en référé afin de demander à la justice d’ordonner la restitution immédiate de son bien.
Une menace bien réelle pour Tesla
Si ce nouvel épisode a tous les ingrédients d’un feuilleton haletant, les répercussions pour Tesla n’ont rien d’un jeu. Dans un secteur où les stocks fonctionnent en « juste-à-temps », l’absence d’une seule pièce peut paralyser toute la chaîne d’assemblage, et c’est exactement ce qui se passe. Au moment de déposer la plainte, Tesla a précisé au juge que ses réserves de pièces s’épuiseraient « en quelques jours ».
Fabriquer de nouveaux outillages prendrait entre 5 et 6 mois pour le constructeur américain tant ses besoins sont spécifiques. Tesla ne peut pas simplement solliciter un autre fournisseur au pied levé pour ces composants. Le constructeur veut récupérer ses machines et a demandé au juge de trancher rapidement.
Selon Tesla, des milliers de véhicules déjà attribués à des acheteurs risquent de voir leur livraison reportée sine die. Angstrom joue sur cette situation pour obtenir un paiement supplémentaire de Tesla afin de débloquer la production.
Si Tesla apparaît ici comme la victime, il faut aussi rappeler que le Cybertruck est produit très loin des volumes promis à l’origine. Un fournisseur dimensionné pour plusieurs centaines de milliers de véhicules par an ne peut probablement pas rester rentable avec les volumes actuels.
Selon les données de Cox Automotive, Tesla n’a livré que 7 263 Cybertruck au premier semestre 2026, une baisse de 32 % par rapport à 2025. La chute est un peu moins marquée au deuxième trimestre (seulement -13 %), certainement aidée par la version plus abordable (à moins de 60 000 $) commercialisée pendant quelques jours par Tesla en février. Il est fort probable que les tensions entre Tesla et son fournisseur ne soient pas aussi récentes que le constructeur voudrait le faire croire.

articles.title: Inflexor Ventures raises Rs 400 Cr as first close of Fund III
articles.text:
Inflexor Ventures raises Rs 400 Cr as first close of Fund III
Fund III will focus primarily on pre-Series A and Series A investments, with initial cheque sizes ranging between Rs 15 crore and Rs 45 crore. The fund aims to build a portfolio of 22–25 companies.
Early-stage, sector-agnostic venture capital firm Inflexor Ventures has announced the first close of its third fund, securing commitments of Rs 400 crore towards its target corpus of Rs 1,250 crore.
The fund, named the Inflexor Technology Discovery Fund, is backed by anchor investors including the Self-Reliant India (SRI) Fund, HDFC Asset Management Company (HDFC AMC), and HDFC AMC Select AIF FoF (HDFC FoF). It has also attracted commitments from several leading international institutional investors, the firm said in a statement.
Fund III will focus primarily on pre-Series A and Series A investments, with initial cheque sizes ranging between Rs 15 crore and Rs 45 crore. The fund aims to build a portfolio of 22–25 companies.
Following the first close, Inflexor Ventures has commenced deployment from Fund III.
This VC firm had previously raised its Fund 1 in 2016 and Fund II in 2021 and has assets under management (AUM) of Rs 1,300 crore with a portfolio of 27 companies. The startups within its portfolio include Atomberg, Kale Logistics, PlayShifu, Entropik, Bellatrix, Clickpost and Cloudsek.
“India's innovation ecosystem has reached an inflection point. We're seeing a growing pipeline of globally ambitious companies built on differentiated science, engineering and technology, creating a compelling opportunity to partner with founders earlier in their scaling journey,” said Venkat Vallabhaneni, Founder and Managing Director of Inflexor Ventures.
According to this VC firm, Fund III will place greater emphasis on Series A opportunities as the Indian venture ecosystem matures and a growing number of companies demonstrate early product-market fit and global scalability.
Inflexor Ventures believes in backing startups that combine technologies and business models capable of compounding value over a decade or more.

articles.title: Microsoft Unveils MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, Its First Cybersecurity AI Model
articles.text:
Microsoft has unveiled its first cybersecurity AI model, MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, which the company claims got significantly better results in finding vulnerabilities than its main competitors.
MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, designed to identify challenging vulnerabilities in complex code, has been integrated into Microsoft’s MDASH multi-agent vulnerability identification and remediation harness.
MDASH orchestrates more than 100 specialized AI agents across multiple frontier and distilled AI models, and has been used to find many vulnerabilities in the tech giant’s own codebases.
According to Microsoft, testing in the CyberGym cybersecurity evaluation framework showed that MAI-Cyber-1-Flash (in combination with MDASH and GPT-5.4) topped Google’s recently launched 3.5 Flash Cyber, OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, and Anthropic’s Mythos 5 in vulnerability discovery.
“MAI-Cyber-1-Flash was designed to efficiently handle up to 90% of all tasks, enabling MDASH to use the larger and most costly models in our fleet (in this case GPT-5.4) for the 10% of exceptionally hard tasks that truly need them,” Microsoft explained.
The company added, “This combination delivers a 50% cost saving when compared against our best offering in MDASH today (GPT 5.4 + 5.4 mini + 5.3 codex). That’s the power of a well-tuned, multi-model system with access to uniquely rich historical training data.”
MAI-Cyber-1-Flash is being offered through Project Perception, an agentic security offering that enables organizations to simulate attacks, detect and investigate threats, and fix vulnerabilities. Project Perception will enter public preview on August 3.
“We see across identities, endpoints, applications, data, clouds and AI systems, providing broad visibility across the digital estate. Equally important, we can help customers take action across those environments,” Microsoft noted.

articles.title: Goutte-à-goutte et inondation : que faire quand la climatisation du voisin ruine votre terrasse ?
articles.text:
Le conflit de voisinage lié à une climatisation commence rarement par le bruit ou l’esthétique. Il commence par une goutte. Un tuyau d’évacuation qui tache une façade, humidifie un garde-corps, rend une terrasse glissante ou finit par s’infiltrer chez le voisin du dessous. En copropriété, cette eau que le climatiseur rejette en continu n’a rien d’un détail technique.
Un climatiseur en marche produit des condensats : l’humidité de l’air se transforme en eau liquide, jusqu’à plusieurs litres par jour en pleine canicule. Peu importe que l’appareil soit mobile, monobloc ou split, le droit ne regarde pas la fiche technique de l’appareil mais ce qui est touché dans l’immeuble. L’article 9 de la loi du 10 juillet 1965 pose la liberté d’usage de son lot, avec une limite nette : chaque copropriétaire doit « ne porter atteinte ni aux droits des autres copropriétaires ni à la destination de l’immeuble ». Une évacuation qui déverse de l’eau sur le balcon d’à côté sort donc du simple confort privé.
Quand les condensats deviennent une atteinte aux parties communes
L’article 25 de la même loi vise les travaux affectant les parties communes ou l’aspect extérieur du bâtiment. Un groupe fixé en façade, un percement, une goulotte visible : toute installation extérieure passe en pratique par un vote de l’assemblée générale. Et poser l’appareil soi-même ne dispense de rien : installer un climatiseur split sans professionnel certifié est déjà encadré dès qu’il y a du gaz à raccorder.
La Cour de cassation a tranché plusieurs fois dans ce sens. Dans un arrêt du 9 juin 2010, la troisième chambre civile rappelle qu’une tolérance de la copropriété ne régularise rien, car « cette ratification implicite suppose l’absence d’équivoque ». Un appareil resté visible plusieurs mois n’est pas pour autant validé. Le 30 mai 2024, la même chambre juge, pour des installations posées sur une terrasse technique, qu’« ils devaient être autorisés par les copropriétaires réunis en assemblée générale », peu importe l’accord donné avant la naissance de la copropriété.
Les condensats ajoutent un trouble matériel à la seule question esthétique : traces blanches, oxydation, humidité, peinture attaquée. Sur ce terrain, l’article 1240 du code civil oblige l’auteur d’un dommage à le réparer, à condition de prouver une faute, un préjudice et le lien entre les deux. Le propriétaire qui invoque son droit de propriété se heurte à l’article 544, selon lequel la propriété ne s’exerce que « pourvu qu’on n’en fasse pas un usage prohibé par les lois ou par les règlements ». Les condensats ne sont d’ailleurs pas la seule source de dispute : l’air chaud soufflé vers le balcon voisin et le bruit du groupe extérieur nourrissent les mêmes conflits.
Locataire, bailleur, syndic : qui répond de quoi
La difficulté grimpe quand l’appareil a été posé par un locataire, dont le voisin ignore souvent le nom. L’article 7 de la loi du 6 juillet 1989 interdit au locataire de « transformer les locaux et équipements loués sans l’accord écrit du propriétaire ». Un percement de fenêtre ou une évacuation fixée en façade dépasse largement l’usage normal. En 2016, la Cour de cassation a rappelé que « le preneur ne pouvait procéder à aucun percement de la façade sans l’autorisation de la copropriété » : l’accord du bailleur ne suffit pas si l’immeuble devait voter.
Le syndicat, lui, peut viser directement le copropriétaire bailleur, qui répond des atteintes provenant de son lot ; à charge pour ce dernier de se retourner ensuite contre son locataire. Le dépôt de garantie n’est pas une sanction automatique : l’article 22 exige des retenues « dûment justifiées », donc des devis, des photos et des états des lieux. Cette grille de lecture juridique vaut autant pour le copropriétaire occupant que pour le voisin qui subit.
Preuves, mise en demeure, référé : les bons réflexes
Le dossier se gagne d’abord sur la preuve. Photos d’ensemble montrant l’appareil, le tuyau et le chemin de l’eau, vidéos courtes et datées, constat de commissaire de justice si le voisin conteste. La mise en demeure doit rester factuelle et viser une action précise : supprimer le rejet d’eau, produire l’autorisation d’assemblée, remettre la façade en état. Une demande limitée à « enlever la climatisation » laisse trop de marge à une réponse partielle. C’est souvent ce courrier ferme qui permet d’obliger un voisin passif à réagir.
En cas d’urgence, l’article 835 du code de procédure civile autorise le juge des référés à « faire cesser un trouble manifestement illicite » ou à « prévenir un dommage imminent ». Un balcon rendu inutilisable en pleine canicule, ou de l’eau qui coule près d’une installation électrique, entrent dans ce cadre. Si l’appareil a déjà été refusé en assemblée, mieux vaut connaître ses recours après un refus d’autorisation avant d’agir en douce. Et quand l’eau a filé chez le voisin du dessous, le sinistre relève aussi de l’assurance dégâts des eaux. À noter : l’article 42 de la loi de 1965 enferme la contestation d’une décision d’assemblée dans un délai de deux mois après notification du procès-verbal.
Le litige apaisé, le climatiseur reste un appareil à piloter avec méthode : faut-il le laisser allumé toute la journée, quel est son vrai poids sur la facture et l’environnement, et le tarif Tempo d’EDF peut-il alléger l’addition sans mauvaise surprise ?
L’objectif concret ne change pas d’un dossier à l’autre. L’eau doit cesser de tomber chez le voisin. Un dossier bien documenté obtient souvent un déplacement de tuyau, une pompe de relevage ou une remise en état sans attendre la fin de l’été. La canicule explique l’urgence d’une solution technique, elle ne justifie jamais d’arroser le balcon du voisin.
